The primary objective of this study was to propose a comprehensive meta-reinforcement learning framework for the adaptive energy management of multi-energy building microgridbalancing electrical and heating loads. The framework integratesan enhanced reptile-based meta-learning algorithm and proximal policy optimization PPO to find a generalized policy for diverse buildings, capable of rapid personalization, improving the sample efficiency and ease of deployment. Two curriculum approaches were developed and compared: Curriculum-1 modeled progressive seasonal complexity, while Curriculum-2 focused on progressive building diversity with constant seasonal exposure. Extensive hyperparameter tuning revealed that models with deeper architectures and the hyperparameter combination significantly impacted learning and adaptation capabilities.
Six high-performing models (3 per curriculum) from the hyperparameter tuning were deployed on five test buildings. The adapted policies achieved a mean reward improvement of 23.9% over the trained meta-policy, with total constraint violations decreasing by 38% and daily operating costs by 12.2%. Curriculum-2 outperformed Curriculum-1 by 53% in terms of mean adaptation improvement and exhibited superior consistency (coefficient of variation < 0.91). The adaptation benefit was statistically confirmed (Wilcoxon W=7162,
\mathtt { p = 1 . 1 1 \times } 1 0 ^ { - 2 0 } )
, with Curriculum-2 outperforming Curriculum-1 across all seasons (19.3% to 36.0%), and winter achieving the largest violation reduction (44%) despite the lowest reward gains. These results demonstrate that learning to build heterogeneity through progressive diversity exposure is more valuable for generalization than sequentially mastering seasonal patterns. The adapted policies showed increased grid dependency as a trade-off for reduced electrical shortages and constraint violations, reflecting an economically rational strategy that prioritizes reliability.

Future work should consider adaptive reward weighting, Hardwarein-the-Loop validation to bridge the simulation-to-deployment gap, adaptive curricula that adjust task complexity based on training performance, and multi-agent coordination for community-scale energy management. A systematic comparison with analytical baselines (MPC, MILP) also represents valuable future work to quantify trade-offs between learned generalization and tailored optimization.

Appendix. Reinforcement learning
Reinforcement learning develops agents that learn optimal decision policies through environmental interaction. In this framework, agents take actions, observe state changes, and receive rewards, learning to maximize cumulative rewards by identifying optimal actions in various states. This approach excels in sequential decision-making problems like energy management in microgrids.
Formally, reinforcement learning operates within Markov decision processes (MDPs), defined as
\mathcal { M } = \left\langle S , \mathcal { A } , P , P _ { 0 } , R , \gamma , T \right\rangle
, where  is the state space,  the action space,
P ( s _ { t + 1 } | s _ { t } , a _ { t } )
the transition probability function,
P _ { 0 } ( s _ { 0 } )
the initial state distribution,
R ( s _ { t } , a _ { t } )
the reward function, 𝛾 the discount factor, and 𝑇 the time horizon. A policy
\pi ( a | s )
maps states to action probabilities. The probability of a trajectory under policy 𝜋 is:
P ( \tau ) = P _ { 0 } ( s _ { 0 } ) \prod _ { t = 0 } ^ { T } \pi ( a _ { t } | s _ { t } ) P ( s _ { t + 1 } | s _ { t } , a _ { t } ) ,\tag{A.1}
The trajectory
\tau = \{ s _ { t } , a _ { t } , r _ { t } , s _ { t + 1 } \} _ { t = 0 } ^ { T }
represents collected data during an episode. The RL objective is to maximize expected discounted return:
J ( \pi ) = \mathbb { E } _ { \tau \sim P ( \tau ) } \left[ \sum _ { t = 0 } ^ { T } \gamma ^ { t } r _ { t } \right]\tag{A.2}
With collected data
\boldsymbol { \mathcal { D } } = \{ \tau ^ { h } \} _ { h = 0 } ^ { H }
from multiple episodes, an RL algorithm functions as
f ( { \cal D } ) \; : \; ( ( \stackrel { n } { S \times { \cal A } } \times \mathbb { R } ) ^ { T } ) ^ { H } \; \rightarrow \; \varPhi
, mapping data to parameterized policies with parameters
\phi \in \varPhi .
Training often employs exploratory intermediate policies rather than purely greedy approaches.
